title: LANDLORD: LONDON 2026 — an homage to Elizabeth Magie's The Landlord's Game (1904)
rules: === A. PREMISE AND FRAMING ===

A1. The game is an original homage to Elizabeth Magie's THE LANDLORD'S GAME (US Patent 748,626, 1904), public domain, which existed to teach the economics of land rent; the strapline on the title screen is 'One board. Two rule sets. Magie was right.'

A2. Every figure rendered on screen must resolve to a key in facts.json; the renderer must refuse to draw a monetary value that carries no `source` field, failing loudly in development rather than printing an invented number.

A3. Each square shows the 2026 assessed value large, and directly beneath it in small caps the 1935 board price (e.g. 'OLD KENT ROAD  £297,500  ·  1935 board price £60'); the contrast is the entire thesis and must never be hidden behind a tap.

A4. Squares are laid out in 1935 board order (cheapest 1935 price first, Mayfair last) while being priced at 2026 values, so the inversion is visible at a glance: Mayfair sits near the trophy corner but is worth less than Whitechapel Road.
A5. One round = one year. Twelve rounds = a twelve-year hold, i.e. one fund life; the game ends in a wind-up and a NAV comparison, not a bankruptcy.

A6. No square, card, token, colour band or corner icon may reference any modern commercial property-trading board game; the banned-terms list in section K is enforced by a build-time string test over all source and content files.
=== B. BOARD LAYOUT ===

B1. The board is a ring of 28 squares drawn as the outer perimeter of an 8x8 grid (4 corners + 6 edge cells per side), leaving a 6x6 hollow centre used for the dashboard; this is the only layout that fits 22 streets plus 6 originals on a 390px phone without scrolling.
B2. Twenty-two squares are the real London streets, carrying real HM Land Registry 2026 values; six squares are original non-street squares.
B3. Index 0 (corner) — THE COMMON. Start square. Movement is clockwise only.
B4. Indices 1,2,3 — streets (1935 ranks 1-3).
B5. Index 4 — THE PLANNING COMMITTEE.
B6. Indices 5,6 — streets (1935 ranks 4-5).
B7. Index 7 (corner) — THE VALUATION OFFICE.
B8. Indices 8-13 — streets (1935 ranks 6-11).
B9. Index 14 (corner) — THE RECEIVER'S OFFICE.
B10. Indices 15,16,17 — streets (1935 ranks 12-14).
B11. Index 18 — THE PUBLIC WORKS.
B12. Indices 19,20 — streets (1935 ranks 15-16).
B13. Index 21 (corner) — THE COMMONWEAL FUND.
B14. Indices 22-27 — streets (1935 ranks 17-22, ending with Mayfair at 27).
B15. Non-street squares break contiguity; the six maximal street runs are therefore of lengths 3, 2, 6, 3, 2, 6.
B16. The holdings panel is called THE REGISTER and uses HM Land Registry structure — Property, Proprietorship, Charges — never a deed-card layout.
=== C. MONEY, SETUP AND THE INHERITANCE ===
C1. Each player starts with STARTING CAPITAL of £2,500,000 in cash.
C2. THE INHERITANCE: streets are ranked 1-22 by 2026 assessed value; Tier A = ranks 1-4 (never dealt, acquisition only), Tier B = ranks 5-11, Tier C = ranks 12-22.

C3. Deal by adjacent-rank pairing: pick k at random such that ranks k and k+1 both lie in Tier B, deal rank k to one player and k+1 to the other by coin flip; repeat independently within Tier C. Each player therefore begins holding exactly two streets, 100% share, unencumbered.
C4. EQUALISATION GRANT: the player with the lower dealt portfolio value receives the exact difference in cash. Adjacent-rank pairing keeps this small; it guarantees identical opening NAV.
C5. The inheritance is framed on screen as unearned: 'You did nothing to earn this land. Neither did anyone else.'
C6. All money is displayed in whole pounds with thousand separators; square faces may abbreviate (£33.5M) but the ledger always shows the full figure.
C7. There is no bank loan of last resort and no cash advance; liquidity comes only from wages, rent, debt against land, the Commonweal Fund, and disposals.
=== D. TURN STRUCTURE ===
D1. A YEAR consists of: Gazette reveal (already face up), Player 1 turn, Player 2 turn, then YEAR END.

D2. On your turn you roll two six-sided dice and choose to advance by die A, by die B, or by A+B — three destinations, always. This single choice is the game's primary skill expression and must be presented as three tappable board highlights, not a menu.
D3. There is no doubles rule, no extra roll, and no square anywhere that causes a player to miss a turn.
D4. Passing or landing on THE COMMON pays WAGES and grants one Right of Pre-emption for that lap.
D5. After moving you resolve the square you ended on (section F), then may take any number of Treasury actions (section G), then end your turn.
D6. The AI turn must resolve and animate within 600ms; there is no 'thinking' state and no network call during play.

D7. YEAR END resolves in a fixed order: (1) passive rent in, (2) land charges out, (3) interest out, (4) shortfall handling, (5) Gazette card resolves and revalues the board, (6) margin call test, (7) Citizen's Dividend if in force, (8) referendum if it is year 6 or 9, (9) next Gazette card revealed face up.
D8. The Year End statement animates in at most 2,500ms as a single scrolling ledger and is skippable by tapping anywhere.
=== E. RENT, THE ENGINE ===
E1. SINGLE DOCUMENTED ASSUMPTION: one gross yield, YIELD_GROSS, applies to every square on the board. No square has a hand-tuned rent.
E2. annualRent(s) = round(assessedValue(s) x YIELD_GROSS).
E3. PASSIVE RENT: at Year End every proprietor receives annualRent(s) x share(s) for every holding, representing the sitting tenant. Property is an income asset whether or not anyone lands on it.
E4. LANDING RENT: if you end your year on a square controlled by your opponent you additionally pay one year's rent as the tenant in occupation.

E5. ASSEMBLY: three or more contiguous street squares controlled by the same player, uninterrupted by a non-street square, form an Assembly. Landing rent inside an Assembly = YIELD_GROSS x (sum of assessed values of every square in that Assembly), not merely the square landed on.
E6. The Assembly rule is what makes cheap streets valuable — Old Kent Road matters because it completes a run — and is the mechanical answer to the 100x spread.
E7. THE RICARDO CAP: rentPaid = max(0, min(rentDue, payerCash - SUBSISTENCE)). A player can never be reduced below one year's wages by rent.

E8. Any rent above the cap is a VOID: it is not owed, not recorded as arrears, and simply evaporates. Rack rent the market cannot bear is the landlord's loss, and the on-screen label reads 'VOID — the tenant cannot pay. Rent is what is left after subsistence.'
E9. Voids are the anti-runaway brake and are economically honest: the landlord's income is capped by the tenant's prosperity.
E10. Ending your year on your own square or on an unowned square you decline triggers no payment.
=== F. ACQUISITION — THE TENDER ===
F1. Ending your year on an unowned street opens THE TENDER.
F2. RESERVE = the square's 2026 assessed value from HM Land Registry.
F3. The landing player nominates one of exactly three prices — Reserve, Reserve x 1.25, Reserve x 1.50 — or Passes. Prices they cannot fund are greyed out.
F4. The landing player simultaneously selects a SHARE of 25%, 50%, 75% or 100%. The residue is taken by THE INSTITUTION, a passive fund that never moves, never bids, and never votes.
F5. Cost to buy = nominatedPrice x share + SDLT(nominatedPrice x share), funded from cash plus any debt raised against the square in the same action.

F6. CUT AND CHOOSE: the opponent then either CEDES (the nominator buys at their own nominated price) or PRE-EMPTS (the opponent buys the same share at that same price, and pays the nominator an Introducer's Fee of 2% of the price). Nominate low and risk losing it cheap; nominate high and secure it dear. One tap each, roughly four seconds.
F7. If the landing player Passes, the opponent may buy at Reserve, at any share, or decline; the square then stays unowned.
F8. You CONTROL a square if your share is 50% or greater. Only controlled squares count towards an Assembly, a referendum land share, or a compulsory purchase target.
F9. Rent on a part-owned square is charged in full to the visitor and split pro rata; the Institution's slice leaves the game permanently.

F10. RIGHT OF PRE-EMPTION (from passing The Common): once per lap you may buy any one unowned street at Reserve x 1.10 plus SDLT without landing on it. This is the pacing valve that prevents a dead game where nobody landed on anything.

F11. INSTITUTIONAL BUYOUT: ending your year on a square you already hold lets you buy out the Institution's residual share at assessed value pro rata plus SDLT. The opponent can never buy the Institution's share in your square.
F12. SDLT is charged on every acquisition including pre-emption, buyout and compulsory purchase, using the real published non-residential band schedule. Churn is expensive because churn is expensive.
=== G. LEVERAGE — THE CHARGES REGISTER ===
G1. Debt is raised against a specific holding, never against the player, and appears in the Charges Register of that title.
G2. maxDebt(s) = floor(assessedValue(s) x share(s) x LTV_MAX). LTV_MAX is the single documented gearing assumption and applies identically to all 22 streets.
G3. On your turn you may borrow up to maxDebt or repay any amount, freely and instantly, on any holding.
G4. Interest is charged at Year End on total debt at BANK_RATE + SENIOR_MARGIN, both real published figures.

G5. Gross yield sits close to the cost of debt, so leverage is NOT accretive from income. It pays only out of the unearned increment — which is precisely Henry George's argument, and the single most important thing the game teaches.

G6. MARGIN CALL: after the Gazette revalues the board at Year End, any holding whose debt exceeds assessedValue x share x LTV_MAX must be brought back within LTV by cash repayment; if cash is insufficient, the game sells the player's lowest-value holding at assessed value less DISPOSAL_COST and repays from proceeds, repeating until compliant.
G7. If land charges and interest exceed cash at Year End, the shortfall is first capitalised as additional debt up to LTV_MAX, and only then triggers a forced disposal under G6.
G8. There is no bankruptcy and no elimination. A player reduced to a single holding still plays, still votes, still collects wages and dividends, and can still win on a late revaluation.
=== H. THE GAZETTE — EVENT DECK AND ITS TRIGGER ===
H1. The deck is THE GAZETTE. Card backs carry a broadsheet masthead; there is no second deck and no personal-fortune deck.

H2. TRIGGER: the top card is revealed FACE UP at the start of each year and resolves at the END of that year, after both players have moved. The market news is public information for a full year before it bites.
H3. Telegraphing the card is deliberate: it converts luck into strategy, since players can gear up ahead of an uplift or deleverage ahead of a crash, and it is exactly how a real cycle behaves.

H4. Twelve MARKET-YEAR cards: each is a genuine historical year of the HM Land Registry / ONS UK House Price Index for London, printed with the year and its actual annual percentage change. Resolving one multiplies every assessed value on the board by (1 + that real percentage).

H5. Six NOTICE cards drawn from real policy and market events, each affecting one player or one square: tenant administration (one year's passive rent voided on your highest-value holding), rating revaluation, an infrastructure consent, a planning refusal, a lender's covenant review (immediate LTV test), and a stock-market shock that raises the cost of debt for one year.
H6. Percentage moves are never invented; every uplift or fall in the game is a real London year with its date on the card face.
H7. The deck is shuffled at setup; only 12 of the 18 cards will resolve in a 12-year game, so the deck differs meaningfully between plays.
=== I. THE SIX ORIGINAL SQUARES ===

I1. THE COMMON (corner, start): pass or land to collect WAGES, being the real ONS median gross annual earnings, and to gain one Right of Pre-emption. The square legend reads 'One year of labour' beside the annual rent of the board's dearest street, so the comparison is unavoidable.

I2. THE VALUATION OFFICE (corner): exercise a COMPULSORY PURCHASE — acquire any one holding controlled by your opponent at assessed value x share x 1.10 plus SDLT, the 10% reflecting the statutory loss payment principle in UK compulsory purchase. This breaks Assemblies and is the sharpest catch-up tool in the game.

I3. THE RECEIVER'S OFFICE (corner): if your portfolio LTV is at or below LTV_MAX you may refinance any one holding free of cost, resetting its debt to LTV_MAX of current assessed value and releasing appreciation as cash; if you are above LTV_MAX you must repay down to it immediately under rule G6. It rewards prudence and punishes gearing without costing anyone a turn.

I4. THE COMMONWEAL FUND (corner): the entire Public Purse is paid out immediately, split EQUALLY between both players regardless of who landed. Under Rack-Rent the purse holds only council tax and the dividend is derisory; under the Single Tax it is transformative. The same square teaching two different lessons is the whole point of Magie's two rule sets.

I5. THE PLANNING COMMITTEE (edge): look at the next two Gazette cards and reorder them. Pure information and control, no dice, no new constants — and an accurate account of who decides which land receives the uplift.

I6. THE PUBLIC WORKS (edge): nominate any one street square; its assessed value rises by INFRA_UPLIFT and the two squares immediately adjacent rise by INFRA_UPLIFT / 2. The owner did nothing; the value rose anyway. The on-screen caption names the beneficiary and reads 'Value created by everyone. Captured by one.'
I7. No original square imprisons, freezes, parks, or skips a player. Dead time is banned outright.
=== J. THE REFERENDUM — MAGIE'S TWO RULE SETS ===

J1. The game begins under RACK-RENT RULES, Magie's 'Monopolist' set: passive rent and landing rent are paid to the proprietor; the proprietor pays only the real council tax for that borough into the Public Purse; there is no tax on gains.
J2. At the end of year 6 both players vote secretly, one tap, on whether to adopt THE SINGLE TAX, Magie's 'Prosperity' set. A second referendum at the end of year 9 may reverse the decision.

J3. Both vote the same way: that is the outcome. On a split vote THE FRANCHISE decides — the player controlling the smaller share of total assessed land value casts the deciding vote, because the land-poor are the many.

J4. Under THE SINGLE TAX: all passive rent and all landing rent is paid to the PUBLIC PURSE instead of to proprietors; council tax is abolished; a BETTERMENT LEVY of 40% is charged on each year's increase in the assessed value of a player's holdings, using the actual rate set by the Land Commission Act 1967; and the whole Public Purse is divided equally between both players at every Year End as the CITIZEN'S DIVIDEND.
J5. Under the Single Tax proprietors keep the land, keep the capital value at wind-up, and keep 50% of the socialised rent; what they lose is the private capture of the unearned increment.

J6. The vote is a genuine dilemma with a computable answer: a player holding a small share of land gains from the Single Tax; a player holding a concentrated share loses. A leader can pre-empt the referendum by deliberately keeping their land share below half — which is itself the lesson.
J7. The referendum screen shows each player's current land share and a live projection of the next year under both regimes, so the choice is informed rather than a coin flip.
=== K. WIN CONDITION AND SCORING ===
K1. The game ends at the end of year 12 with THE WIND-UP.
K2. NAV = cash + sum over holdings of (assessedValue x share) - total debt. Highest NAV wins.
K3. Tie-breaks in order: most controlled squares; then longest single Assembly; then the player who voted for the Single Tax.
K4. MERCY RULE: from the end of year 6, if one player's NAV is at least three times the other's the game ends immediately, to prevent a decided game from grinding out six dead years.

K5. The end screen decomposes each player's total gain into three attributed figures — WAGES EARNED, RENT COLLECTED, and UNEARNED INCREMENT (revaluation) — and states the third as a percentage of total gain. In practice it will dominate, and that number is the game's actual payload.

K6. The end screen also shows the 1935 versus 2026 ranking table for all 22 streets, with the rank changes marked, and one factual line noting that the 1935 ladder spanned about 6.7x while the 2026 values span over 100x.
=== L. THE AI OPPONENT ===
L1. The AI is a deterministic linear-utility heuristic evaluated in under five milliseconds. There is no language-model call, no search tree and no simulated deliberation delay.

L2. MOVEMENT: score each of the three destinations and take the maximum plus epsilon noise. Unowned street: U = 0.55 x normalisedValue + 0.30 x assemblyGain + 0.25 x gazetteAlignment - 0.40 x fundingStrain. Opponent-controlled: U = -1.0 x (landingRentDue / max(cash, 1)). Own square: U = +0.05. The Common: +0.30. The Valuation Office: +0.45 if a compulsory purchase target is affordable, else +0.05. The Receiver's Office: +0.35 if LTV <= LTV_MAX, else -0.50. The Commonweal Fund: +0.20 + 0.6 x (purse / NAV). The Planning Committee: +0.25. The Public Works: +0.40 if it controls a two-square run, else +0.15.

L3. NOMINATION: compute affordability A = cash + availableDebt - reserve for next Year End (interest + land charges + 10% buffer). If reserve > A, Pass. Otherwise nominate Reserve x 1.50 when the face-up Gazette card is an uplift of +5% or better or the square completes an Assembly and A >= 1.5 x reserve; Reserve x 1.25 when the opponent's cash exceeds the reserve, so contest is likely; Reserve otherwise.
L4. SHARE: choose the smallest share that both secures control (>=50%) and leaves at least 20% of NAV in cash; drop to 25% only for Tier A trophies it cannot otherwise touch.

L5. PRE-EMPTION: pre-empt when nominatedPrice <= 0.85 x its own valuation, where its valuation = assessedValue x (1 + expected Gazette uplift) x 1.25 if the square completes an AI Assembly, and the purchase is affordable under L3.

L6. GEARING: target LTV 0.30 by default; 0.55 when the face-up Gazette card is +5% or better; 0.10 when it is -3% or worse; never above LTV_MAX. Repay pre-emptively at Year End if projected post-shock LTV would breach LTV_MAX.
L7. VOTE: choose the Single Tax if its controlled land share is below 45%, or if its NAV is below 85% of the opponent's; otherwise Rack-Rent.
L8. PUBLIC WORKS: nominate the square maximising (own value gain including the two neighbours) - 0.5 x (opponent value gain).
L9. COMPULSORY PURCHASE: take the opponent holding maximising (value of the Assembly it breaks + own Assembly gain), subject to affordability at value x 1.10 + SDLT.
L10. PLANNING COMMITTEE: reorder the two upcoming cards so that the more positive one resolves in the year in which the AI's projected LTV is highest.
L11. DIFFICULTY is a single epsilon on the utility scores: Surveyor 0.35, Fund Manager 0.15, Freeholder 0.00. No other numbers change, so difficulty never cheats on money.
=== M. IMPLEMENTATION AND COMPLIANCE ===

M1. facts.json is the sole source of truth and must carry, per street: id, displayName, assessedValue2026, valueSource, valueDate, borough, councilTaxBandD, councilTaxSource, boardPrice1935. Globally it must carry yieldGross with its derivation, bankRate, seniorMargin, ltvMax, sdltBands, wagesMedian, infraUplift, disposalCost and the Gazette year series, each with a source string and a retrieval date.
M2. A unit test must assert that every monetary constant used by the engine resolves to a facts.json key, and that no numeric literal representing money appears in the game logic.

M3. Target session length is under 10 minutes on a phone at 12 years, 2 players, leaving headroom against the 12-minute ceiling; a timing test must fail the build if a scripted playthrough exceeds it.
M4. Human input per turn is at most three taps: die choice, tender response, optional treasury action. There is no free-text entry and no numeric keypad anywhere in the game.
M5. Board cells render at roughly 46px on a 390px viewport; the 6x6 centre carries cash, NAV, LTV, the face-up Gazette card and the year counter, all visible without scrolling.

M6. BANNED STRINGS, enforced at build time across all files: the trademarked name of the modern commercial property game, its mascot's name, 'Community Chest', 'Chance', 'Title Deed' card layout, 'Go to Jail', 'Free Parking', 'Boardwalk'. Banned visually: any mascot character, top-hat or motor-car token, the classic banded colour-group card header, red and yellow card backs, and the four classic corner icons.
M7. Player tokens are original surveying instruments — a ranging rod and a theodolite — not characters or vehicles.

M8. The credits screen states: 'After THE LANDLORD'S GAME by Elizabeth Magie Phillips, US Patent 748,626, 1904. Public domain. Property data: HM Land Registry Price Paid Data and UK House Price Index, Open Government Licence v3. 1935 board prices cited as historical fact for comparison.'
antiPatterns: RUNAWAY LEADER — do not let a single trophy acquisition decide the game. The Ricardo cap (rent is bounded by the payer's surplus above subsistence) and the equal-split Commonweal Fund are the structural brakes. Never add a 'rent doubles' or 'rent x10' multiplier on top of the yield; the Assembly rule is the only rent amplifier and it is additive, not multiplicative.

FORCED BANKRUPTCY SPIRAL — never eliminate a player. Shortfalls capitalise into debt first, then trigger a single forced disposal at assessed value (no fire-sale discount beyond the documented 1.5% disposal cost). A player down to one holding must still be able to win on a late Gazette revaluation, or the last four years are theatre.

DEAD TIME — no missed turns, no imprisonment, no 'wait three turns', no square that does nothing. Every one of the six original squares grants an action. The Receiver's Office deliberately gives the prudent player a free refinance rather than punishing the unlucky one.

AI THINK TIME — no language-model call, no minimax, no artificial 'thinking...' delay. The heuristic must resolve in under 5ms and animate in under 600ms. Latency destroys a 10-minute phone game faster than any balance problem.
PURE DICE — a turn that offers no choice is a wasted turn. The two-dice / three-destinations rule must never be simplified to a single die 'for clarity'; it is the primary skill expression.
TYPING — no free-text bids, no numeric keypad. The three-rung nomination ladder exists precisely so that price discovery costs one tap.

INVENTED NUMBERS — never hand-tune a square's rent 'for balance'. One yield, one LTV, applied identically to all 22 streets. If the balance is wrong, change the yield, the starting capital or the turn limit, never a single square. A per-square fudge destroys the traceability claim that is the whole reason this game is defensible.

FLATTENING THE SPREAD — do not compress the 100x range into a tidy ladder, and do not apply a concave rent curve. The re-ordering is the intellectual content. Handle the spread with fractional shares, the Ricardo cap and the Assembly rule, not by editing reality.

DEAD TROPHY SQUARES — if the four Tier A assets can never be bought, a fifth of the board is decoration. Fractional JV shares at 25% exist specifically so the £33.5M asset is reachable by year four, and the balance test must confirm a Tier A square trades in at least 60% of simulated games.
DEAD GAME FROM BAD DICE — a player who lands on nothing buyable for six years has no game. The Right of Pre-emption at The Common is the pacing valve; do not remove it as 'redundant'.

TRADE DRESS BY DRIFT — the risk is not the first draft, it is the fourth. Watch for a mascot creeping into the title screen, corner squares acquiring familiar icons, property cards growing a banded colour header, or a designer 'improving' the board to 40 squares. The 28-square ring, original corner names and Register-style holdings panel are compliance features, not styling choices.
TUTORIAL WALL — do not gate play behind a rules explanation. The regimes, the tender and the referendum must teach themselves through one-line captions at the moment they first fire.

SANCTIMONY — the Georgist point lands through mechanics and real data, not lecturing. One factual caption per event, never a paragraph. The end-screen unearned-increment percentage does more persuading than any text could.

SLOW YEAR END — nine sequenced steps can easily become a fifteen-second interruption twelve times over, which alone would blow the time budget. Cap the ledger animation at 2.5 seconds and make it skippable.

REFERENDUM AS COIN FLIP — if players cannot see what the Single Tax will do to them, the vote is noise. The referendum screen must show live land shares and a projection of the next year under both regimes.
concreteValues:
"=== GAME PARAMETERS ===
STARTING_CAPITAL   = 2_500_000            // £ cash per player
TURN_LIMIT         = 12                   // years; 1 round = 1 year = one fund life
PLAYERS            = 2                    // 1 human vs 1 AI by default
BOARD_SQUARES      = 28                   // 8x8 ring: 22 streets + 6 originals
SUBSISTENCE        = WAGES                // rent floor; a player never falls below one year's wages
MERCY_RULE         = 3.0                  // from end of year 6, NAV ratio that ends the game
SHARE_OPTIONS      = [0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00]
CONTROL_THRESHOLD  = 0.50                 // share needed for Assembly / vote / CPO eligibility
NOMINATION_RUNGS   = [1.00, 1.25, 1.50]   // multiples of Reserve
INTRODUCER_FEE     = 0.02                 // paid to the nominator when pre-empted
PREEMPTION_PREMIUM = 1.10                 // Right of Pre-emption from The Common
CPO_PREMIUM        = 1.10                 // Land Compensation Act statutory loss principle
ASSEMBLY_MIN       = 3                    // contiguous controlled streets
GAZETTE_DECK       = 18                   // 12 real London market years + 6 notice cards
AI_EPSILON         = {surveyor: 0.35, fundManager: 0.15, freeholder: 0.00}

=== FACTS-FILE CONSTANTS (every one a real published figure; defaults shown must be overwritten from facts.json at build time) ===
YIELD_GROSS   = (ONS_London_mean_monthly_private_rent * 12) / UKHPI_London_average_price
              // THE single documented assumption. Default 0.0480 (4.80%). One yield, all 22 streets.
LTV_MAX       = 0.60                      // UK senior CRE convention; the single gearing assumption
BANK_RATE     = 0.0400                    // Bank of England Bank Rate, facts.json, dated
SENIOR_MARGIN = 0.0175                    // published senior debt margin, facts.json, dated
DEBT_RATE     = BANK_RATE + SENIOR_MARGIN // = 0.0575 default. Note: DEBT_RATE > YIELD_GROSS by design.
WAGES         = 37_430                    // ONS median gross annual earnings, facts.json
SDLT_BANDS    = [ {to:150_000, rate:0.00}, {to:250_000, rate:0.02}, {to:Infinity, rate:0.05} ]
                                          // real published non-residential / mixed-use schedule
COUNCIL_TAX[borough] = real Band D charge, per borough, per year (Westminster's is famously the lowest —
                                          this is the Georgist punchline, printed, not invented)
INFRA_UPLIFT  = (UKHPI_London_avg_today / UKHPI_London_avg_10y_ago) ^ (1/10) - 1
                                          // one real year of London's own historic growth
GAZETTE_YEARS = [ {year, pctChange} ]     // 12 genuine UKHPI London annual changes, printed with dates
BETTERMENT    = 0.40                      // Land Commission Act 1967 rate; Single Tax regime only
DISPOSAL_COST = 0.015                     // agency + legal, market convention
BOARD_1935[street] = 60 … 400             // historical board prices, display and end-screen only

=== DERIVATION FORMULAE (arithmetic, implement verbatim) ===
annualRent(s)        = round( assessed(s) * YIELD_GROSS )
passiveRent(s, p)    = round( annualRent(s) * share(s, p) )
assembly(s, owner)   = maximal run of contiguous street squares controlled by owner containing s,
                       uninterrupted by a non-street square; if length < ASSEMBLY_MIN then { s }
landingRentDue(s, p) = round( YIELD_GROSS * SUM( assessed(t) for t in assembly(s, owner(s)) ) )
rentPaid(due, p)     = max( 0, min( due, cash(p) - SUBSISTENCE ) )
void(due, p)         = due - rentPaid(due, p)          // evaporates; never recorded as arrears

maxDebt(s, p)        = floor( assessed(s) * share(s, p) * LTV_MAX )
interest(p, year)    = round( totalDebt(p) * DEBT_RATE )
ltv(p)               = totalDebt(p) / SUM( assessed(s) * share(s, p) )

sdlt(price)          = 0.02 * max(0, min(price, 250_000) - 150_000)
                     + 0.05 * max(0, price - 250_000)
reserve(s)           = assessed(s)                      // HM Land Registry 2026 value, unmodified
acquisitionCost(s, rung, share)
                     = (reserve(s) * rung * share) + sdlt( reserve(s) * rung * share )
preemptionCost(s, share)
                     = (assessed(s) * PREEMPTION_PREMIUM * share) + sdlt(assessed(s) * PREEMPTION_PREMIUM * share)
cpoCost(s, share)    = (assessed(s) * share * CPO_PREMIUM) + sdlt( assessed(s) * share * CPO_PREMIUM )
disposalProceeds(s, p)
                     = round( assessed(s) * share(s, p) * (1 - DISPOSAL_COST) ) - debt(s, p)

revalue(card)        : for every street s -> assessed(s) *= (1 + card.pctChange)
publicWorks(target)  : assessed(target) *= (1 + INFRA_UPLIFT)
                       assessed(target-1) *= (1 + INFRA_UPLIFT / 2)

landCharge_rackRent(s, p)  = COUNCIL_TAX[borough(s)] * share(s, p)
landCharge_singleTax(s, p) = passiveRent(s, p)                            // 100% of land rent to the Purse
bettermentLevy(p)          = round( BETTERMENT * max( 0, SUM( (assessed_end(s) - assessed_start(s)) * share(s,p) ) ) )
                                                                          // Single Tax regime only
citizensDividend(p)        = floor( publicPurse / PLAYERS )               // paid at every Year End under Single Tax,
                                                                          // and on landing on The Commonweal Fund

equalisationGrant(p)       = maxDealtPortfolioValue - dealtPortfolioValue(p)
NAV(p)                     = cash(p) + SUM( assessed(s) * share(s, p) ) - totalDebt(p)
unearnedIncrement(p)       = SUM of all revaluation gains credited to p over the game
                             ( reported at wind-up as a % of p's total gain )

notes:
"HOW THE 1904 HERITAGE SHOWS UP IN THE MECHANICS, not just the credits:

1. TWO RULE SETS ON ONE BOARD. Magie published her game with two sets of rules — 'Monopolist', where rent enriches one player and grinds the rest down, and 'Prosperity', where land rent goes to the public and everyone gains. That duality is not decoration here; it is the referendum at the end of year 6 and again at year 9, and it is the single largest strategic decision in the game. The same board, the same squares and the same dice produce two entirely different economies, which is exactly the demonstration Magie built.

2. THE RICARDO CAP IS THE LAW OF RENT, IMPLEMENTED. Rent is capped at the tenant's surplus above subsistence, and anything above it is a void that simply evaporates. That is the classical law of rent — rent is the residual after subsistence — stated as a line of code rather than a lecture. It also happens to be the cleanest possible anti-runaway and anti-bankruptcy device, which is a nice demonstration that Magie's economics were also good game design.

3. NOBODY IS ELIMINATED, THEY ARE GROUND DOWN. Under the Monopolist rules Magie's point was never that the loser dies; it is that the loser is reduced to the margin and stays there, permanently, while doing exactly as much work as before. A player at subsistence in this game still moves, still votes, still collects wages, and can still be rescued by a revaluation or by winning the referendum. That is a more uncomfortable and more accurate ending than bankruptcy.

4. THE UNEARNED INCREMENT IS THE ONLY REAL PROFIT. The yield sits just below the cost of debt, so leverage cannot be paid for out of rent. All the money in the game comes from revaluation — Gazette cards carrying real London market years, and The Public Works square raising the value of land whose owner did nothing. The end screen states each player's unearned increment as a percentage of their total gain. That figure is the argument.

5. WAGES ARE ON THE BOARD AND THEY ARE PITIFUL. Magie's start square was about labour producing wages. Ours pays the real ONS median gross annual salary and prints it beside one year's rent on the board's dearest street. No commentary is required; the two numbers are both real and the ratio does the work.

6. THE INHERITANCE IS UNEARNED. Players do not start with an empty board. They are dealt land they did nothing to acquire, which is how land actually gets held, and which gives the georgist critique its opening position rather than a level playing field that never existed.

7. THE PUBLIC PURSE AND THE CITIZEN'S DIVIDEND. The Commonweal Fund pays out equally to both players regardless of who landed on it. Under Rack-Rent the purse contains only council tax and the dividend is embarrassing; under the Single Tax it contains the whole land rent and is decisive. The same square delivers both halves of the argument without a word of text.

8. THE COUNCIL TAX JOKE IS REAL AND IT IS THE BEST FACT ON THE BOARD. Each square carries its borough's actual Band D charge. Westminster's is among the lowest in the country while its land is the dearest, so a £33.5M Mayfair holding pays a smaller land-related tax than a flat on Old Kent Road. That is not satire, it is the published rate, and it is the strongest single piece of evidence for Magie's case that the game can show without editorialising.

9. SELF-INTEREST DECIDES THE VOTE. The referendum is not a morality test. A land-poor player gains from the Single Tax and a land-rich player loses, and the screen shows both projections. Players reliably vote their position, which reproduces the actual political economy of land taxation more honestly than any argument would.

10. LEGAL SEPARATION IS A DESIGN FEATURE. The 28-square ring, the six original corner and edge squares, the Register-style holdings panel, the Gazette deck and the surveying-instrument tokens all exist partly because the 1904 lineage is public domain and the 1935 lineage is not. Leaning into Magie rather than around her is both the cleaner legal position and, as it turns out, the better game."
